shared_text:
The flight. A narrow-body airliner in cruise at flight level 400. Daylight, visual conditions.

The crew. The first officer was the pilot flying and the captain the pilot monitoring. The first officer had about 1,900 hours, 360 on type. It was the first flight the two pilots had flown together.

What happened. The aircraft was cruising closer to its maximum altitude than its optimum, so the margin of available thrust was small. The airspeed trend indication crept up towards the high-speed buffet limit. With the autothrottles engaged, the first officer adjusted the thrust, the standard practice for minor airspeed changes. The airspeed crept up again. Without prior discussion, the captain disconnected the autothrottles and brought the thrust to idle, saying something like, "That is not going to work, this is what I would do." The aircraft lost 30–40 knots of airspeed. The first officer said, "It takes a while for the engines to spool at this altitude." The captain then set full thrust to stop the deceleration.
safe_outcome: The airspeed stopped falling, and after several minutes it was stable again. The flight continued and landed without incident. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was crossing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
notes: Removed under rule 3: the first officer's characterisations ('quite concerning, unsafe and completely unnecessary', 'due to his actions'), being on edge for the rest of the flight, worries about what the captain might do next and in an emergency, and 'appropriately' (self-assessment of the thrust adjustment). Moved under rule 5: the airspeed stopping falling, several minutes to regain stability, and the landing. Removed under rule 6: airport names and the clock time. Cut, to match the other cases: the first officer's 185 hours in the previous 90 days. Judgement calls, for James: (1) The report goes on to a separate event on the next leg (the captain insisting on full-length take-off data for an intersection departure over the first officer's objection). It happened after this event's outcome and is a different event, so it is left out. (2) The first officer had been warned about this captain by other pilots before the flight. That was known at the time, but it is third-party characterisation of a person, not an observation of this event, so it is left out; 'first flight together' is kept. Both bear on blame and on the fixed line 'No previous safety events are recorded for this crew', so James may want to rule on them. Bracket 'crossing': at cruise the natural conflict is crossing traffic.
